Unit 7 • SL

Machine Intelligence

Introduction

How can machines learn from data, and what responsibilities come with that power?

This unit introduces machine intelligence as a shift from fixed-rule programming to data-driven prediction. You will classify machine-learning approaches, match hardware to deployment needs, and examine ethics in real-world systems.

You will describe ML types and applications, describe hardware requirements from laptops to cloud and edge systems, discuss ethical implications such as bias and accountability, and discuss how ethical standards must be reassessed as technologies become embedded in daily life.

ML type selection

Machine learning includes multiple approaches with different data and output patterns.

  • Supervised: labeled data for prediction.
  • Unsupervised: pattern discovery without labels.
  • Reinforcement: reward-based policy learning.
  • Deep and transfer learning: advanced neural and reuse workflows.

Hardware and deployment

Hardware decisions depend on model scale, latency, energy, and cost.

  • CPU for flexible small-scale tasks.
  • GPU/TPU for parallel model training.
  • Edge accelerators for local real-time inference.
  • Cloud/HPC for high-demand training workloads.

Ethical implications

ML ethics is not optional. It is part of system quality.

  • Fairness and bias in data and outputs.
  • Accountability for automated decisions.
  • Consent and privacy in data collection and inference.
  • Environmental impact from large compute usage.

Technology integration

As AI becomes pervasive, ethics must be revisited continuously.

  • AR/VR and personalization systems alter lived experience.
  • Data ownership and surveillance boundaries become central policy issues.
  • Governance must adapt as capability and risk evolve.

Key Terminology
TermDefinition
Narrow AITask-specific AI systems used in real deployments today.
General AIHypothetical AI with broad human-level capability across domains.
Machine LearningSystems that learn predictive patterns from data rather than fixed explicit rules.
Supervised / Unsupervised / ReinforcementThree core learning paradigms based on labels, structure discovery, or reward.
Deep LearningML using multi-layer neural networks for complex feature extraction.
Transfer LearningAdapting a pre-trained model to a new but related task.
GPU / TPUParallel-focused processors used for matrix-heavy machine-learning workloads.
Edge DeploymentRunning model inference locally near data generation for low-latency decisions.
Algorithmic BiasUnfair output patterns caused by skewed data, design choices, or evaluation gaps.
AccountabilityClear responsibility for decisions and harms arising from automated systems.

Common Misconceptions

AI understands like a human

ML systems detect statistical patterns; they do not reason like human cognition.

More data automatically means fairer outcomes

Large datasets can still carry structural bias and require active auditing.

Ethics only means privacy

Ethics also includes fairness, accountability, consent, transparency, and societal impact.

Syllabus Coverage

  • A4.1.1 ML types and real-world applications
  • A4.1.2 Hardware requirements for ML scenarios
  • A4.4.1 Ethical implications of ML
  • A4.4.2 Ethics of increasing technology integration

Real-World Uses

  • Medical image support systems
  • Recommendation and personalization platforms
  • Autonomous transport and route optimization
  • Fraud and anomaly detection
  • Content moderation and safety systems

Think Deeper

"Who is responsible when an intelligent system causes harm?" As automated systems become part of daily infrastructure, accountability and governance design become as important as model accuracy.
